episodes.203896: Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts, which damaged powerlines near College Station.
episodes.203897: Marine Thunderstorms produced strong wind gusts.
episodes.203927: During the late afternoon and early evening of the 4th, slow moving thunderstorms produced heavy rainfall and flooding to portions of west-central and southwest central Indiana.  Flooding was most significant in southeastern Vigo County near Blackhawk where a video showed flash flooding of a field and nearby road.  Later in the day, flash flooding also occurred in Daviess County and Lawrence County with two major roads flooded.  Total rainfall estimates were as high as 3-5 inches in these areas.
episodes.203998: An MCS pushing through east-central Texas and into South Texas this mid-day outperformed expectations at least this far south. Guidance had suggested the bulk of the activity to stay north/east of our area, but more organized convection transpired rather than just the isolated to scattered activity previously expected. An outflow pushing out ahead of the convection led to marine thunderstorm winds.
episodes.204119: A supercell severe thunderstorm tracked south from eastern Morgan county to  Washington County and then into Lincoln County. The storm produced very large hail across Lincoln County, up to three inch diameter hail.
episodes.204786: Weak low-to-mid level troughing, differential heating, and upslope flow contributed to the development of thunderstorms across West Texas and Southeast New Mexico. A couple of thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts before dissipating after dark.
episodes.205168: Scattered afternoon thunderstorms developed in a summertime airmass with a couple of severe storms occurring in Lowndes county with impacts to trees and power lines.  In addition, a very moist airmass and weak steering flow led to flash flooding across portions of southwest Georgia.
episodes.205173: Scattered thunderstorms resulted in several measured wind gusts in excess of 34 knots.
episodes.205375: Several severe storms moved across southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska, dropping large hail and producing severe wind gusts.
episodes.205444: An anomalously moist airmass, with precipitable water values between 0.8 and 1.0+ inches, was established across the region. A passing shortwave trough provided large-scale lift, triggering widespread thunderstorms with very high rainfall rates. The overall environment supported training convection, where multiple storms repeatedly moved over the same areas. These conditions were highly favorable for producing excessive rainfall and initiating flash flooding.
episodes.205600: Southwest steering pushed a stronger west coast sea breeze inland through the day with a sea breeze merger near the I-95 corridor in the afternoon where a few stronger storms developed, then moved offshore producing gusty winds.
episodes.206136: A pair of mesoscale convective systems impacted portions of western Oklahoma on the 3rd, once during the early morning hours and then again during the mid-evening. Occasional observations of severe winds occurred with each convective system.
episodes.206450: An upper-level trough moved over western Kansas early in the morning. Correlating with a PVU maximum and left exit region of the jet aloft, plenty of dynamical support was present for strong storms to develop producing all hazards. This included a weak and brief tornado, 4 inch hail, and 85 mph winds. This manifested in a couple supercells and a small bowing MCS moving southward across SW Kansas.
episodes.206526: A weak trough of low pressure triggered a few clusters of thunderstorms across central and southeast Illinois during the afternoon and evening of August 4th.  One of the most prominent clusters dropped 2.44 of rain in a short amount of time at the Lawrenceville Airport and caused flash flooding along Illinois Route 1 on the north side of Lawrenceville.
episodes.206569: A weak cold front moved into and stalled across North Texas, serving as a focus for scattered shower and storm development over the first few days of August as upper level disturbances moved overtop the region. The storms were slow-moving and some became severe, producing damaging winds and hail. The highest wind gust occurred in the early morning hours of August 4th, when a microburst over the DFW ASOS produced an 89 mph wind gust (the strongest on record at that ASOS). Between the 1st and the 4th, there were many reports of damaging winds, and one report of 1 inch hail near Euless.
episodes.206576: Scattered thunderstorms on the afternoon of August 3rd produced large hail and caused flash flooding in Lyman County. Heavy rainfall from these storms led to a trained spotter reporting water flowing over roads in West Brule.
episodes.206664: A shortwave trough and closed low reached the Quad State from the northwest during the morning of the 4th. The arrival of the shortwave preceded peak heating by several hours, limiting convective potential. Shear was very weak and instability limited. Slow-moving storms did produce torrential rainfall, with flooding issues reported in Hamilton County.
episodes.206779: A tornado moved through a rural portion of northern Osceola County.
episodes.206893: The combination of a stationary front lingering across the area along with deep moisture nearby led to thunderstorms capable of producing heavy rainfall and flash flooding across Southeast Georgia.
episodes.207057: Two rogue storms produced hail across the Black Hills and in the eastern plains.
episodes.207098: A isolated supercell developed within northwest flow over the region and trekked southward across Bent and Las Animas Counties, dropping significant hail during its lifespan.
episodes.207131: Isolated strong to severe thunderstorms developed across the Concho Valley and Northern Edwards Plateau. A few severe storms produced damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.207546: On August 3rd, an incoming upper level trough was positioned west of eastern Oregon and an associated cold front moved across eastern Oregon. Thunderstorms developed ahead of and along the cold front as it moved west to east. Model soundings indicated a dry boundary layer (inverted-V soundings) in eastern Oregon during convective initiation.

KMLB radar data indicates the circulation, along with a corresponding debris signature, moved east over a densely wooded area before subsequently lifting around 18:22 LST, just west of Storey Bend Rd. ||Given limited access to the affected area, the track is considered approximate, and an EF rating cannot be provided.
